title: With the Samanas

teacherSummary.text: With the Samanas, Siddhartha learns fasting, enduring pain, and meditations that let his self pass into animals and objects. Yet after three years he concludes these are only escapes from the self, not true release. When rumors spread of Gotama, the Buddha, he and Govinda leave; Siddhartha masters the old Samana with his gaze before departing.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “With the Samanas,” how does Hesse show self-denial as a path? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the theme you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how With the Samanas develops the idea of self-denial as a path. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses theme in With the Samanas to complicate the reader's understanding of self-denial as a path. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate With the Samanas within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of self-denial as a path responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads With the Samanas as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of self-denial as a path. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

satQuestions.passage: Silently, Siddhartha exposed himself to burning rays of the sun directly above, glowing with pain, glowing with thirst, and stood there, until he neither felt any pain nor thirst any more. Silently, he stood there in the rainy season, from his hair the water was dripping over freezing shoulders, over freezing hips and legs, and the penitent stood there, until he could not feel the cold in his shoulders and legs any more, until they were silent, until they were quiet. Silently, he cowered in the thorny bushes, blood dripped from the burning skin, from festering wounds dripped pus, and Siddhartha stayed rigidly, stayed motionless, until no blood flowed any more, until nothing stung any more, until nothing burned any more.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Siddhartha calls the Samanas' practices a 'brief numbing.' Do you agree? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include numbing, nirvana, festering, cowered, numbness. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “It is fleeing from the self, it is a short escape of the agony of being a self, it is a short numbing of the senses against the pain and the pointlessness of life.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: Enfeebled in, or destitute of, the power of sensation and motion.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Asceticism—strict self-denial—was a widespread spiritual practice in ancient India. Now, why does this chapter matter? Siddhartha discovers that discipline alone can become another form of illusion, a key turn in his quest. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Theme, Characterization, Imagery.

I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
